newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Swedish property market shows glimmer of life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swedish property market shows glimmer of life.

text.p: Sweden's real estate market is laying the foundations of a new structure after reemerging from the rubble left by the property collapse of the early 1990s, analysts said.
Analysts said the sector had bottomed and was starting to take slow and cautious steps forward but was still trailing the rest of the stock market.

But they said the new-look market is shaping up to be far more focused on the home market than before with Swedish players starting to streamline their portfolios and divest themselves of large stakes in foreign property.
"Swedish real estate firms need to restructure their portfolios, mainly because they are so diversified," said an analyst at Handelsbanken.
"After the 1980s many firms saw that they couldn't manage properties all over Europe. They have to concentrate and be good on the local market."
With over 30 property companies currently listed on the Stockholm bourse, analysts said the sector was ripe for rationalisation. After that it could start to look attractive.
"What you'll see in the future is fewer, larger companies," a property analyst from broker Matteus told Reuters.
"With a lot of finance deals and mergers, once you have larger more consolidated property companies, you will probably see more foreign interest in buying."
The nation's banks are leading the drive to streamline portfolios.

Four Swedish banks, S-E-Banken, Handelsbanken, Swedbank and Foreningsbanken, have this year started to trim their operations, spinning off property divisions, to concentrate on their core business, banking.
This move was prompted after the government late last year scrapped the heavy tax burden banks had to pay if they wanted to get rid of the property stakes they inherited.

One consequence of the troubles of the loan-loss crisis that swept across the Swedish banking system in the early 1990s was that the banks found themselves with huge real estate holdings, taken over as collateral on bad loans.
Swedbank's former property division, Tornet, was independently quoted on the Stockholm bourse in early May and Handelsbanken's former property company, Nackebro, was listed in June.

These two companies were among the highest climbers on the bourse list in August, with Tornet climbing to 75 crowns in August from a start of 56.50 crowns and Nackebro reaching 96 crowns from 82 crowns.
S-E-Banken's Diligentia, Sweden's largest property company with holdings worth around 25 billion crowns ($3.78 billion), is set to be launched on the Stockholm bourse later this year.
Property analyst Fredrik Grevelius from Swedish brokerage house Carnegie said Diligentia is set to sell 50 percent of its holdings abroad.
"Diligentia will sell off 50 percent of its holdings, mainly abroad, although they might keep some holdings in Brussels," Grevelius told Reuters.

Only Foreningsbanken has yet to spin off its real estate division, Mandamus, to shareholders but it has announced plans to sell off its properties in Sweden and abroad, worth a total of 3.5 billion crowns by the end of 1998.

Sweden's other big bank, Nordbanken, had its troubled loans put into a separate company, Securum, in 1992 after being bailed out by the state in the wake of the loan-loss crisis following the property excesses of the 1980s.
In July this year Morgan Stanley bought a 60 percent stake in Castellum, the property arm of Securum, which was formed by the government to liquidate Nordbanken's troubled loans.
But analysts say although the sector has started to move, it is still trailing the market overall and the restructuring is just paving the way for future moves.
The construction and real estate index has risen eight percent since the start of 1996 while the general index has climbed 20 percent during the same period.

For the first half of 1996, Swedish property giant Skanska reported first half-year net profits of 1.6 billion crowns compared to 926 million crowns a year ago and NCC posted first half-year net profits of 189 million crowns against three million crowns last year.
"I don't think much will happen on the price side for real estate but what could happen is that real estate shares will rise because they are traded at high direct yields," Grevelius said.
Analysts said overseas interest in Swedish property would start to grow once the sector was looking in better shape.
"Foreign investors in the property market are looking for quality, large companies with good position concentrated in the Stockholm area," said the Matteus analyst. ($1=6.617 Swedish Crown)
